patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent episodes of staring and unresponsiveness, sometimes with repetitive hand and mouth movements, occurring approximately twice monthly for the past eight months
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Kapoor is a 35-year-old right-handed male high school chemistry teacher who presents for inpatient evaluation of recurrent episodic spells of altered awareness that have been occurring approximately twice monthly over the past eight months. He was referred by his primary care physician after his wife witnessed two distinct episodes and became increasingly concerned.

The patient himself has limited recall of the events. He reports that on several occasions at work, colleagues have told him he appeared to suddenly stop mid-sentence while lecturing, stared blankly for what seemed like a minute, and then seemed confused for several minutes afterward. He did not fall during any of these episodes and had no preceding warning that he could recall. His wife has witnessed two episodes at home. During the most recent event two weeks ago, he describes his suddenly becoming unresponsive while they were watching television. He appeared to make repetitive chewing motions with his mouth and was picking at his shirt with his right hand. She called his name repeatedly but he did not respond. The episode lasted approximately 60 to 90 seconds, after which he appeared disoriented and asked her what had happened. He seemed confused for about five minutes before returning to his baseline. He noted that his speech seemed slightly slurred during the recovery period.

When specifically asked, the patient is uncertain whether he experiences any preceding sensations, though he notes that on a few occasions he has had a brief feeling of something being oddly familiar, which he attributed to distraction or daydreaming. He has never had a generalized convulsion, tongue bite, or urinary incontinence during any episode. He denies any preceding headaches, visual disturbances, lightheadedness, or palpitations. He reports feeling more fatigued recently and has had some difficulty concentrating at work, which he attributes to poor sleep related to his untreated sleep apnea and work-related stress. There has been no recent weight change, fever, or other systemic complaints. His anxiety has been stable on sertraline.

results.title: Quantitative MRI in temporal lobe epilepsy: relationship with neuropathology and surgical outcome
results.summary: Automated hippocampal volumetry detected subtle hippocampal atrophy in 30% of visually MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy patients, correlating with histopathological hippocampal sclerosis and favorable surgical outcomes.

results.title: Subtle hippocampal malformations and volumetric reduction in temporal lobe epilepsy
results.summary: Quantitative volumetric analysis can reveal hippocampal sclerosis not visible on standard visual MRI interpretation, supporting the use of automated tools in epilepsy presurgical evaluation.

results.title: FDG-PET in MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy: lateralizing value and surgical outcomes
results.summary: FDG-PET demonstrated temporal hypometabolism in 70-80% of MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy patients, with good surgical outcomes when PET and EEG were concordant.

output.summary: In patients with temporal lobe epilepsy and subtle or initially negative MRI findings, quantitative hippocampal volumetry and FDG-PET provide important additional lateralizing information. Automated volumetric analysis can detect hippocampal sclerosis missed on visual inspection in up to 30% of cases. FDG-PET lateralizes the epileptogenic zone in 70-80% of MRI-negative cases. Multi-modal concordance (EEG, MRI volumetrics, PET, neuropsychology) is essential for surgical planning and predicts favorable postoperative seizure outcomes.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin with subtle mesial temporal sclerosis (focal impaired-awareness seizures)

differential.key_features: Distinguished by video-EEG capturing event without electrographic correlate; current semiology with automatisms and amnesia favors epilepsy.
Lacks hypermotor or nocturnal features; oroalimentary automatisms and post-ictal confusion favor temporal localization.
Absences are shorter (<20 s), without post-ictal confusion, and have 3-Hz generalized spike-wave on EEG.
No postural prodrome, no documented bradycardia or hypotension; semiology is not syncope-like.
TIA produces negative neurological symptoms (weakness, aphasia), not stereotyped behavioral arrest with automatisms.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura, automatisms, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with temporal-lobe aura and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; subtle memory deficit may be present.

optimal_actions.action: Order EEG (routine first; pursue ambulatory or video-EEG if non-diagnostic) to identify interictal epileptiform discharges and capture habitual events.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal sharps/spikes and/or focal slowing in the anterior temporal region; ictal correlate confirms diagnosis.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI through the hippocampi).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hippocampal sclerosis, low-grade tumor (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, or focal cortical dysplasia; rule out alternative structural causes.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if drawn within 10–20 min of event), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic provocation (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, uremia); baseline organ function for AED selection; AED level for adherence and dosing.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for AED selection in focal epilepsy and ILAE 2017 seizure classification.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evidence-based AED options for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide); ILAE classification framework.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating or modifying AED therapy (enzyme inducers, OCP, other CNS-active drugs).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify pharmacokinetic interactions (CYP induction by carbamazepine/phenytoin) and CNS adverse-effect overlap.

optimal_actions.action: Pursue prolonged video-EEG monitoring to capture habitual events, confirm lateralization, and evaluate surgical candidacy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Capture of habitual focal seizure with electrographic correlate; concordance with imaging supports surgical workup.

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological battery to lateralize memory function and inform surgical risk.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Material-specific memory deficit consistent with side of seizure focus (verbal memory deficit in dominant TLE; visuospatial in non-dominant).

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when semiology is clearly epileptic.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting epileptogenic substrates (hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, low-grade tumor) and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause influences AED choice (e.g., low-grade tumor → consider AEDs with CYP-neutral profile; hippocampal sclerosis → multiple equally appropriate options). MRI should inform drug selection.

critical_actions: Recognize recurrent stereotyped behavioral arrest with automatisms and amnesia as focal impaired-awareness seizures.
Obtain prolonged video-EEG to capture a habitual event and confirm focal temporal onset.
Order 3T MRI epilepsy protocol to look for hippocampal sclerosis or other epileptogenic substrate.
Initiate first-line AED for focal epilepsy after diagnosis confirmation.
Counsel on driving restrictions and seizure safety.
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture without features of CNS infection.
Do not rely solely on a single normal routine EEG to exclude epilepsy.
Do not start a broad-spectrum AED such as valproate without considering focal-epilepsy first-line options.
key_reasoning_points: Frequency of ~2 episodes/month over 8 months meets ILAE epilepsy criteria (≥2 unprovoked events).
Routine EEG sensitivity is limited; prolonged monitoring or sleep-deprived EEG increases yield.
Imaging-negative TLE still benefits from dedicated 3T epilepsy-protocol MRI; some lesions are subtle.
Cross-modal concordance is the diagnostic gold standard before considering surgical evaluation.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.
